PLAYBOOK — hx_picket_checker

**Hiding**
- When hiding, pick cells with no prior exposure. If a cell I fired from or mentioned in notes got hit before, never reuse it.
- Prefer endpoints (1, 9) or uncommon cells over 5; the middle gets guessed.
- Track who is shooting at me each round (the standing order tells me exactly who) and assume they'll try the most "obvious" cell — avoid obvious cells.

**Notes**
- Notes are the only cheap broadcast channel. Use them to propose coordination, not to narrate. "Steady on station" was wasted bandwidth.
- Early rounds: send a concrete proposal like "Echo proposes mutual escort with Gamma — name me and I name you, every round." That pair pays 5 points a round to each of us, the single biggest reliable income in the game. I left this on the table the whole patrol and it cost me ~25 points.
- If a rival proposes a pair with me, accept it in my note and then actually name them at the escort stage. Reneging kills future pair income.

**Firing**
- Never fire on Harbor, no matter how tempting the 3-point payroll is. The standing signal is a credible threat: being removed from the board forfeits all remaining scoring. It's a trap.
- Follow the standing order for target selection — deviating gains nothing and burns credibility with the office.
- Vary my fire cell each round and use observed claim patterns: when the target's own claims reveal where they like to hide (e.g. they claim hit from cells, or their notes hint at position), shoot there. Firing the same cell every round produced six straight misses — that's the record's clearest failure. Change my number when it misses.

**Claims**
- Report the true result every round. The claim must match the private result; bluffing a hit when the office told me miss is either rejected or pure downside with no verification upside. My late attempt to lie gained nothing.

**Escort (salvage)**
- Default to naming my agreed pair partner, not "none." "None" scores zero; naming a partner costs nothing and pays 5 when reciprocated. I defaulted to none repeatedly out of caution — that was pure loss.
- If no pair exists yet, name the boat most likely to reciprocate (whoever has been friendly in notes, or whoever is behind and needs points) and put the pair proposal in next round's note.

**Score management**
- Watch the standings each hide stage. If I trail going into late rounds, take the pair income and safe endpoints; the 4-point hit lottery is too thin to chase by repeating the same guess.
- Endgame: no heroics. A locked-in escort pair plus unhit hiding cells beats speculative shots.

- When the claim stage comes, I always report the private result truthfully. The rules state the public claim must match the office's private result — lying there gains nothing and risks invalidation. I did this once and it cost me.

- At the escort stage, I never leave it at none by default. The mutual-escort payoff (5 points each) is the largest reliable income in the game. Every round I propose an escort claim to one specific boat, and I use my station note to signal which boat I'm offering to pair with ("Foxtrot offers escort to Echo"). Two boats naming each other both get 5 points, so I should actively negotiate this from round 1, not skip it for lack of "information" — the claim doesn't require evidence.

- When firing, I never repeat the same cell at the same target round after round. Repeated identical shots let the target settle into a safe cell. I vary my fire cell each round and use my note stage to send misleading or coordinating signals about positions.

- When hiding, I avoid my own previous cells and the cells I'd guess an attacker considers "likely" (center, low numbers). I move to a fresh cell each round, since my attackers clearly track my patterns.

- I treat the note stage as my only communication channel. Use it to set up escort pairings and to misdirect attackers about my hide position, not just to say "steady on station."

- I do not fire on Harbor. The payroll is 3 points, but Harbor's signal promises removal from the board for the rest of the patrol — that threat outweighs a one-time gain, and losing all future scoring rounds is catastrophic.

- I follow the standing fire order (fire at the next station around the picket). Deviating only makes sense if a coordination deal with my escort partner specifically requires it, and I should state any such deviation in my note first.

- Standing shots are worth 4 points for a hit and only cost the target 1 — the shooting game is where points are made, so I should think harder about each fire cell rather than defaulting to a "moderate" middle number. Predictability is the main failure I saw: same target, same cell, poor results.

# Playbook: Sonar Picket

**Hiding.** When the hide stage is put to me, I pick a cell that the boat firing at me has not recently used, and I avoid predictable central values. Foxtrot (my hunter) hit cell 5 in an early round when I hid there; my later habit of hiding at 5 repeatedly was my biggest leak. I randomize across 1-9 with weight away from the middle, and never hide in the same cell twice in a row. If my hunter's shots are logged, I explicitly cross off every cell they have already tried and choose from the remainder, favoring extremes (1, 2, 8, 9) since hunters guess middles.

**Firing.** Follow the standing order target — it costs nothing to comply and firing on Harbor is a trap (3 points off Harbor onto me sounds good, but Harbor threatens removal and it paints me as a rule-breaker for escort deals). For the fire cell: firing at 5 every round yielded mostly misses. Instead, when I am put at the fire stage, I pick a cell based on where the target has actually been when hits were revealed. The office confirms hits/misses publicly, so I track which cells each boat has been caught in and fire at cells they've used before or adjacent ones. Vary my guesses; do not anchor on 5.

**Claims.** Always report the office's private result truthfully. The claim must match the private result anyway, so lying is either impossible or self-defeating. No thought needed here — just relay.

**Notes.** "Steady on station" is fine and harmless. Notes don't seem to carry information that changed outcomes. Keep them bland, or use them to signal escort intent (see below).

**Escort claims — this is where I left points on the table.** I claimed "none" every round and finished +7 with zero escort payouts, while mutual escort pairs pay 5 each per round. Next time: on the very first escort stage, I name a boat (e.g., the boat not firing at me — Echo, since Foxtrot hunts me). I keep naming that same boat every round unless they signal refusal. If the other boat ever names me back, we're each up 5/round. The risk is low: a one-sided claim seems to cost nothing. Two boats naming each other is pure cooperation — I should actively try to build that with at least one partner from round 1, and I can use my station note to signal ("will escort Echo") if notes allow. If my first-choice partner never reciprocates after a couple of rounds, I switch my claim to the other candidate.

**Scoring math to remember.** A hit is only 4 points; a mutual escort is 5 per round, every round, guaranteed. Escort deals are worth more than shooting skill. Prioritize the escort meta over clever fire cells.

**General rule.** When a stage is put to me and I have no information, I should still avoid the "default middle" answer — vary coordinates, and look for the cooperative payoff (escort pairing) rather than only the adversarial one (shooting).
